summaries: The work addresses the problem of determining an unknown conductivity distribution within a domain given boundary measurements and noise. A finite element method is proposed, incorporating regularization and mesh refinement to improve stability and accuracy in the reconstruction process. Numerical results in one and two dimensions demonstrate the method's effectiveness in recovering both the exterior and interior conductivity, alongside an analysis of its sensitivity to noise and discretization choices. The approach culminates in convergence proofs for the reconstructed conductivity and potential fields.

The study investigates the permutations generated during Gaussian elimination with partial pivoting (GEPP) when applied to various random matrices. Researchers analyze the permutation patterns arising from the factorization of scalar butterfly matrices and classify them within specific permutation groups, demonstrating deviations from uniformity for Gaussian orthogonal and unitary ensembles. The work also highlights the impact of implementation details, such as the norm used for pivot selection, on the resulting pivot probabilities and establishes a link between random matrix theory and permutation combinatorics.

The work addresses the difficulties in numerically simulating kinetic schemes due to the infinite support of the Maxwell velocity distribution function. Researchers propose utilizing a hat function, initially introduced by Perthame, as a compact alternative to the Maxwellian, which allows for a simplified numerical analysis. This approach enables a direct proof of the scheme's positivity and facilitates the development of higher-order accurate solutions. Numerical experiments demonstrate the scheme's effectiveness in solving inviscid flow problems.

The study addresses the simulation of magnetic phenomena using a finite-element method, focusing on the Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equation. A specific time integration scheme, based on a backward differentiation formula of order two, is adapted to handle additional physical effects and improve computational efficiency through implicit-explicit splitting. The authors establish a theoretical result demonstrating the convergence of the numerical solution, removing restrictive constraints on the time step size. Validation through numerical experiments confirms the effectiveness of the proposed method.

The paper addresses the challenge of generating samples from probability distributions defined by unnormalized densities, a common problem in statistical inference and machine learning. The authors develop an iterative algorithm based on a novel application of the Wasserstein--Fisher--Rao Jordan--Kinderlehrer--Otto (WFR JKO) scheme, which approximates the Kullback--Leibler divergence. They demonstrate theoretical convergence guarantees for the scheme and implement it using reweighted normalizing flows, achieving strong empirical results on complex distributions.

The study addresses limitations in existing Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) architectures when representing high-frequency components in partial differential equation solutions. The authors introduce CAFE+FNO, a novel approach that utilizes Content-Aware Frequency Encoding+ (CAFE+) to generate Fourier kernels by combining Fourier and Chebyshev features through multiplicative composition and affine branches. Experimental results on several PDE benchmarks demonstrate improved performance compared to existing FNO variants, with ablation studies confirming the effectiveness of the proposed components.

The work addresses the solution of elliptic PDEs on complex domains using a finite element method. A novel approach is presented, utilizing polynomial splines on hierarchical T-meshes to handle domains implicitly defined by level-set functions. The method minimizes a residual over an extended neighborhood, enabling implementation on a background mesh and avoiding complex geometric constructions. The study provides theoretical error estimates and demonstrates the method's accuracy and efficiency through numerical experiments.

The paper addresses the challenge of creating a systematic approach for constructing multiple orthogonal polynomials, particularly when extended to multiple dimensions. The authors propose a generalized method based on Koornwinder-type techniques, introducing coupling schemes to combine different polynomial families. This results in explicit formulations of multiple orthogonal polynomials on various geometric domains, including bounded and unbounded regions in two and higher dimensions, and provides a framework for generalizing these constructions to higher dimensions.

The work addresses the challenge of accurately simulating nonlinear wave systems, particularly those with complex constitutive relationships. Researchers developed a novel space-time discretization strategy employing discontinuous Galerkin methods and Petrov-Galerkin techniques to achieve high-order accuracy and maintain energy/entropy stability. Numerical experiments demonstrate the scheme’s ability to preserve key physical properties like energy conservation and maintain nonnegative dissipation, even with discontinuities.

The work addresses the challenge of efficiently solving a coupled finite element and boundary element method system arising from a scattering problem. A new formulation is presented, based on trace spaces and operators, to eliminate interior degrees of freedom and create a system amenable to preconditioning. The authors then construct a block-diagonal preconditioner derived from the Maxwell single layer boundary integral operator, demonstrating a bounded spectral condition number and validating its performance through numerical tests.

The work addresses the challenges of constructing accurate interpolations on spherical surfaces, particularly when dealing with triangles that are distorted due to radial projection. A novel approach is taken by separating the effects of anisotropy and radial distortion through factorization of the element map. The analysis yields precise formulas for geometric properties and allows for the adaptation of planar interpolation techniques to the spherical setting, ultimately demonstrating the optimality of certain transfer factors and directional bounds.

The study addresses the simulation of coupled physical phenomena involving mechanical deformation, electric fields, and magnetic fields within a solid material. A finite element method is constructed using specialized element spaces designed to avoid numerical instability and allow for computations on complex geometries. The method incorporates a technique to decouple the influence of material properties from the error analysis and an explicit update scheme for the magnetic field to improve computational efficiency. Results from numerical tests are presented to validate the proposed approach.

The work addresses the challenge of efficiently simulating systems governed by both hyperbolic and parabolic partial differential equations. A novel numerical scheme is developed, integrating an explicit leapfrog method for the hyperbolic component with an implicit Crank–Nicolson method for the parabolic component, employing a Strang-type splitting. This approach relaxes the typical time-step restrictions associated with parabolic problems, leading to a scheme governed by a less stringent hyperbolic CFL condition. The authors provide theoretical error analysis and validate the method's performance through numerical simulations.

The study addresses limitations in existing physics-informed neural network methods for solving partial differential equations, which often struggle with solutions exhibiting varying complexity. The authors propose a novel approach, Representation Capacity Adaptation for PDEs (ReCAP), that dynamically adjusts the network's structure during training by redistributing computational resources based on localized physics residuals. Experiments on several three- and four-dimensional problems demonstrate that ReCAP significantly outperforms existing methods, achieving a substantial reduction in solution error.

The study addresses the simulation of crack growth influenced by temperature changes, combining heat transfer and material deformation. A novel computational approach utilizes neural networks to represent temperature and displacement fields, incorporating a sharp crack representation and enriching the displacement near crack tips. The method minimizes energy functionals and extracts stress intensity factors to predict crack propagation paths, demonstrating agreement with established solutions in various test scenarios.

The study addresses the challenge of efficiently solving evolution equations arising in optimal control problems, specifically within the context of open quantum systems. Researchers developed a sequential quadratic Hamiltonian (SQH) method to solve the continuous optimality system, utilizing second-order exponential midpoint propagators for the forward and adjoint equations. They introduced both full-rank and low-rank schemes to maintain the Hermitian and positive-semidefinite properties of the density matrix, alongside rigorous error analysis and validation through numerical experiments demonstrating convergence and efficiency.

The study addresses the computational estimation of thermodynamic properties for systems governed by specific Hamiltonian structures. A quantum simulation approach is proposed, combining state preparation, Trotterization, and quantum signal processing to determine partition functions and observables. Numerical validation using the Hubbard model demonstrates the potential for improved computational efficiency compared to classical methods, particularly for certain parameter regimes.

The study investigates the stability of a specific type of neural network architecture, focusing on the properties of the matrices formed during the network's operation. Researchers employ mathematical analysis, including differential operators and coefficient recovery estimates, to derive bounds on a key measure of stability, the condition number. The analysis reveals a relationship between the network's complexity, represented by the feature count, and the condition number, demonstrating exponential growth with a dependence on dimensionality. Numerical experiments corroborate the theoretical findings, providing insights into the impact of normalization techniques.

The work addresses the problem of approximating functions within a bounded domain using a specific type of neural network architecture. The authors develop a construction method for shallow neural networks with predetermined activation functions and parameters, ensuring independence from the target function. They demonstrate that the resulting approximation error decreases at a rate proportional to $N$ to the power of negative $(s-m)/d$, establishing optimality based on Sobolev width lower bounds. Numerical validation is performed to assess the $L^2$ and $H^1$ approximation capabilities in two and three dimensions.

The study addresses the simulation of fluid interfaces exhibiting surface tension effects, employing a finite element method to track the evolving boundary. A novel arbitrary Lagrangian-Eulerian (ALE) formulation is introduced, incorporating a compensated tangential velocity to maintain mesh quality during deformation. The resulting scheme demonstrates energy stability and temporal consistency, validated through numerical experiments showing improved mesh preservation compared to existing techniques.

The study addresses the approximation of Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman equations, a class of nonlinear partial differential equations, on domains extending to infinity. Two distinct methodologies are explored: a mesh-free approach utilizing Wendland kernels and a physics-informed neural network technique. The research establishes error bounds based on empirical residuals, demonstrating convergence on compact sets and providing quantitative error estimates dependent on discretization parameters and regularity assumptions. Ultimately, the work aims to provide a theoretical framework for understanding and controlling the accuracy of these approximation methods.

The paper investigates methods for approximating complex functions with specific logarithmic behavior on sectors. Researchers developed a lightning-plus-polynomial approximation technique, incorporating a one-sided Abel--Poisson formula and contour integration to establish error bounds. They also derived an explicit formula for the representation dimension, demonstrating how to control the number of poles required for accurate approximation, and validated these findings through numerical experiments.

The study investigates the approximation of a function using rational functions with a repeated pole, focusing on a specific geometric region. Researchers employed techniques including Möbius maps, contour deformation, and saddle expansions to analyze the error in the approximation. The analysis reveals a sharp asymptotic estimate for the error, demonstrating a dependence on a scaling parameter and a geometric factor, and recovers known results in specific cases. Numerical experiments and theoretical bounds are used to validate the findings and explore the behavior of the approximation in different scenarios.

The study addresses the challenge of developing boundary conditions for the compressible Navier-Stokes equations that maintain stability and adhere to thermodynamic principles in numerical simulations. Researchers constructed a new isothermal no-slip wall boundary condition using summation-by-parts and simultaneous-approximation-term operators to enforce temperature and velocity constraints at the wall while preserving entropy production. The resulting formulation demonstrates design-order accuracy and stability through validation on established benchmark problems for compressible flow.

The study addresses the challenge of efficiently computing the inverse of a differential operator, a task often encountered in solving partial differential equations. A decomposition strategy is employed, separating the Green's function into a known singular part and a remaining harmonic extension operator, which is then learned using reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces. This approach demonstrates significant improvements in both the algebraic input rate and the output rate, transitioning from algebraic to exponential convergence, and is extended to handle nonlinear problems through iterative decomposition.

The authors developed SAGE-PINN, a novel framework that incorporates axisymmetric geometry and parity-preserving variable transformations to eliminate singularities and enforce mass conservation, alongside staged training and boundary-fitted analytical functions to stabilize the optimization process. Validation against finite element solutions for nanofluid flow in a stenosed artery demonstrated accurate predictions of axial velocity and temperature within 1.6% and 9.1% relative L2 error, respectively, across a wide range of flow and thermal conditions. The authors conclude that embedding geometric and physical constraints directly into the network architecture provides a robust approach for simulating axisymmetric multiphysics flows.

summaries: The study investigates the behavior of a fundamental linear algebra algorithm when applied to randomly generated matrices. Researchers employed probabilistic arguments to establish a lower bound on the likelihood of a specific performance characteristic, demonstrating a significant deviation from previously held expectations. The analysis reveals that the probability of substantial growth in the algorithm's operations follows an exponential decay rate dependent on the matrix size and the magnitude of the growth itself.

The work addresses the challenge of finding Moore-Penrose inverses for matrices with rational function entries, a problem complicated by the non-linearity inherent in the Penrose conditions. The authors leverage the properties of fields with an involutory automorphism to simplify the computation, bounding the degrees of the resulting pseudoinverse and identifying parameter values where the inverse fails. The research culminates in symbolic algorithms implemented in Maple and tested extensively, demonstrating their applicability to economic modeling.

The study addresses the computational burden associated with solving heterogeneous partial differential equations that vary with parameters. A method is proposed that combines the multiscale generalized finite element method with geometric interpolation techniques, specifically targeting the efficient computation of local approximation spaces. By representing optimal subspaces as points on a Grassmann manifold and approximating them using sparse grid interpolation, the method aims to reduce the dimensionality of the problem and improve computational efficiency. Results from numerical experiments on elliptic problems demonstrate the convergence properties of the proposed approach.

The work investigates methods for choosing a subset of columns from a large matrix to minimize a specific norm related to the submatrix's pseudoinverse. The researchers developed a new deterministic algorithm, Forward derandomized volume sampling, which offers a significant improvement in computational complexity compared to existing approaches, particularly for matrices where the number of columns is much larger than the number of rows. This algorithm achieves a theoretical bound on the objective function and is demonstrated to be effective through numerical experiments across various applications.

The study addresses the simulation of heat transfer within complex composite structures, specifically those found in electronic packaging. Researchers devised a computational method utilizing a cut finite element approach, which allows for the representation of intricate geometries on a simplified background mesh. The method incorporates specialized techniques to accurately model temperature and heat flux at material interfaces and to handle intersections between elements. Numerical experiments involving realistic electronic packaging designs demonstrated the method's accuracy and computational efficiency.

This work investigates a novel filtering technique for images, adapting the median filter to a continuous-time setting. The researchers developed a method that progressively reduces noise and demonstrate that, as the filter's parameters approach a specific limit, the process converges to a known geometric flow equation. The study establishes a strong convergence of energies, a significant advancement for this class of filtering schemes, and utilizes a compensated compactness approach to achieve the result.

The study addresses the challenge of efficiently simulating systems governed by Partial Differential Equations (PDEs) when the initial conditions are not fixed. Researchers extended the Latent Dynamics Network (LDNet) architecture, which combines Neural Ordinary Differential Equations with dimensionality reduction, to handle variable initial states by inferring the initial latent state from early-time observations. Two strategies were explored: an auto-decoding formulation and a meta-learning approach, both demonstrating improved accuracy and a structured latent space representation. The resulting framework offers a resolution-independent surrogate modeling solution for many-query simulations.

This paper addresses a discrepancy between theoretical predictions and observed behavior in the construction of bivariate splines. The authors investigate the dimensionality of a specific space of splines defined on a triangular mesh, focusing on cases where the mesh exhibits particular geometric properties like collinearity and invariance under symmetry transformations. They demonstrate a counterexample to a conjecture proposed by Strang, showing that the dimensionality of the spline space exceeds the predicted value for a carefully constructed triangulation.

The study investigates a method for advancing solutions in time, particularly for problems where the solution moves quickly. The researchers developed a new scheme, AdHImEx, that combines explicit and implicit time integration to maintain stability for large time steps while preserving accuracy. Results show the scheme achieves second-order accuracy and requires only one matrix solve per time step, demonstrating improved performance compared to existing approaches and exhibiting promising efficiency for atmospheric simulations.

The study addresses the challenge of accurately simulating the evolution of interfaces in materials, a process described by partial differential equations. Researchers developed a new computational technique that integrates a specific time-stepping scheme with a neural network to represent the solution without relying on a traditional grid. The resulting solver demonstrates stable behavior and improved performance compared to other neural network-based methods, as validated through numerical tests.

The study addresses the challenge of accurately simulating geometric flows, which describe the evolution of curves and surfaces over time. Researchers developed a new time integration method based on implicit-explicit Runge-Kutta schemes, adapting existing finite element formulations to represent the problem as a system of ordinary differential equations. The resulting schemes achieve second and third-order temporal accuracy while minimizing the need for separate geometry prediction steps and requiring only linear solvers at each stage. Numerical tests confirm the accuracy of the methods and demonstrate comparable mesh quality to simpler approaches.

The work addresses the challenge of developing neural networks that natively respect the mathematical structure of differential forms, specifically focusing on spaces related to divergence and curl. The authors define new neural approximation classes directly within these spaces, avoiding reliance on traditional mesh-based or finite element methods. This approach enables the creation of a novel numerical method, FOSLS-deRhaNN, which leverages these classes to solve a variety of partial differential equations, including those with discontinuous coefficients and complex boundary conditions.

The work addresses the challenge of efficiently approximating solutions to differential equations involving complex operators. A technique of dividing exponential functions into smaller components is explored, leading to a reduction in computational demands. The study establishes theoretical convergence results for specific numerical methods based on this splitting approach, and these results are validated through simulations on two example equations.

The study addresses the optimization of a stochastic algorithm used for Bayesian inference, focusing on the selection of a subsampling rate within a multilevel framework. The researchers developed a cost-error criterion to determine an efficient subsampling rate, balancing errors across different levels of resolution and avoiding overly conservative choices. This criterion is based on estimates of variances, autocorrelation times, and per-level computational costs, and is validated through numerical experiments on elasticity beam and Darcy-flow problems, demonstrating significant computational cost reductions.

The study addresses the limitations of the Navier-Stokes equations when describing fluid behavior under conditions where the continuum assumption breaks down. Researchers developed a machine learning approach to construct a generalized model that bridges the gap between the Navier-Stokes equations and the computationally expensive Boltzmann equation. This involved training a model to predict non-equilibrium variables based on equilibrium variables and the Knudsen number, using data generated from Boltzmann equation simulations, and employing a specialized learning technique to minimize error accumulation. The resulting generalized model demonstrated improved accuracy in several benchmark fluid dynamics problems.

The work addresses the challenge of optimizing resource allocation in hierarchical data structures, specifically within a diffusion imaging context. A novel approach, Learned Adaptive Multiresolution Diffusion Imaging, is proposed, which integrates a learned policy to dynamically adjust the resolution hierarchy during processing. Experimental results demonstrate a reduction in a discrepancy metric and an increase in occupancy compared to a deterministic baseline, alongside observations about the stability of energy usage during the learning process. The method's adaptability and transferability to higher resolutions are also highlighted.

The work addresses the problem of approximating trigonometric polynomials within a specific norm using a finite set of sample points. A constructive approach is employed, combining de la Vallée Poussin sampling operators and Smolyak-type identities to generate explicit norming sets with controlled size and constant. The research establishes bounds on the size of these sets and provides probabilistic guarantees for random point configurations, while also demonstrating limitations on the achievable size of norming sets under certain constraints.

The study investigates methods for solving the radiative transfer equation, a complex problem arising in various scientific and engineering fields. Researchers developed modified iterative solvers, incorporating adaptive accuracy control and a hybrid sampling strategy to improve efficiency and handle multiscale scenarios. The new approaches reduce computational costs by adaptively adjusting ranks and reusing angular bases, while also preserving the integrity of Krylov subspace methods. Numerical experiments on benchmark problems validated the effectiveness of the proposed techniques.

The study addresses challenges in controlling derivative growth when approximating functions using kernels that span multiple scales. Researchers developed interval inverse inequalities for spaces built from kernels exhibiting positive exponential spectra, focusing on managing boundary effects and interactions between different scales. They employed techniques like synthesis-operator perturbation and adjacent-derivative comparison to achieve coefficient bounds that are largely independent of the number of scales and their positions, demonstrating a lower bound approaching 1/2. Numerical examples using Cauchy and logistic kernels illustrate the stability of coefficients in various multiscale setups.

The work addresses the numerical solution of advection-reaction-diffusion equations framed within a specific geometric setting, utilizing a novel scheme based on the JKO method. The proposed approach leverages neural networks to parameterize spatial maps and mass-changing factors, enabling the simultaneous handling of spatial redistribution and mass variations. The study demonstrates the existence of minimizers, establishes bounds on their behavior, and provides conditions for energy dissipation, alongside a discrete Euler-Lagrange equation. Numerical validation confirms the scheme's accuracy and explores the interplay of different physical processes.

The study investigates the sensitivity of approximate solutions to the optimal transport problem, particularly when the cost is close to the minimum possible value. Researchers analyze how small perturbations in the input data affect the resulting transport map, considering unbounded domains and specific moment conditions on the source density. The analysis reveals a sharp conditioning modulus that depends on parameters related to the problem's dimensions and constraints, with implications for the accuracy of common map estimation techniques and improvements over existing stability results.

The study addresses the numerical solution of a partial differential equation arising in financial modeling, specifically for pricing derivatives. A finite element method based on B-splines and scaling functions is proposed, incorporating a tempered stable process that introduces unique challenges due to its non-local and asymmetric properties. The authors focus on developing efficient algorithms and deriving rigorous error estimates, demonstrating the method's accuracy and stability through comparisons with established techniques and calibration to market data. The resulting discretization allows for rapid pricing of options and American-style derivatives, alongside the calculation of sensitivities.

The work addresses the problem of efficiently approximating linear operators when only forward operator-vector products are accessible. The authors develop a new algorithm that leverages local row-space information and high-order regularity estimates to achieve query-efficient approximation without relying on adjoint operator access. The resulting algorithm uses a logarithmic number of randomized queries to achieve a specified error tolerance in the Hilbert-Schmidt norm, demonstrating improved performance compared to existing methods.

The study addresses the challenge of finding solutions to nonlinear partial differential equations, specifically focusing on those exhibiting quasi-periodic behavior. Researchers developed a numerical method based on alternating schemes and a novel observation regarding resonant equations, circumventing traditional coordinate transformations. The method’s implementation required adapting multiscale induction to an additional dimension, necessitating careful control of excluded frequencies and addressing issues arising from spatially separated sites with identical temporal indices. Numerical validation demonstrated the scheme's ability to compute quasi-periodic solutions and confirm iterative convergence.

The work investigates a method for determining material behavior from velocity measurements within a system governed by partial differential equations. A novel neural network architecture, ICNNE, is developed to learn a dissipation potential, ensuring the resulting mathematical model remains stable and generalizable. The approach combines finite element and neural network techniques to enforce convexity and other physical constraints within the learned potential, enabling accurate predictions and generalization across various flow regimes. Results demonstrate the ability to recover known physics, transfer to new geometries, and avoid numerical divergence in challenging scenarios.

summaries: This paper investigates the growth factor, a key indicator of numerical stability during Gaussian elimination, for random matrices. The authors employ techniques from random matrix theory and smoothed analysis to derive precise estimates for the growth factor, both with and without pivoting strategies. A central result resolves a long-standing conjecture by demonstrating that the growth factor for Gaussian matrices with partial pivoting is typically bounded by the square root of the matrix dimension, $n$. These findings also enhance the understanding of the growth factor's behavior under partial pivoting through a refined smoothed analysis.

Neural PDE solvers can sometimes fail to converge to an accurate solution as parameters increase indefinitely, resulting in unattainable best-loss approximations. This paper investigates this phenomenon in deep neural networks using translated kernels, identifying that missing limits arise from unbounded parameters or redundant neurons. The authors recover these missing functions by incorporating kernel derivatives into the model, enabling the attainment of the best possible approximation. Numerical experiments then examine parameter growth and the impact of this completion on PDE optimization.

The paper addresses the challenge of quantitatively understanding how families of variational functionals converge, a process crucial for analyzing numerical approximations and inverse problems. The authors develop a new framework combining variational convergence with interpolation theory, introducing "variational $K$-functionals" to characterize convergence rates and establish compactness extrapolation theorems. This approach provides explicit convergence rates for minimizers and is applied to image processing models like ROF, revealing a connection between image regularity and convergence rates measurable through Brezis-Van Schaftingen-Yung spaces. The resulting method unifies and extends existing results in related areas of the Calculus of Variations.

This paper investigates how to ensure accurate behavior at junctions in networks modeled by the time-fractional heat equation, which describes heat and mass transport in complex media. The authors use Laplace transforms and numerical simulations to analyze the interaction of waves at the vertex of a star-shaped graph, revealing a relationship between incoming and outgoing wave properties. They demonstrate that a key condition for preventing unwanted reflections, known as the diffusion-coefficient sum rule, holds true regardless of the fractional order of the time derivative, suggesting that the memory effect of the transport law does not influence junction transparency.

The study investigates the surface Stokes-Cahn-Hilliard system, which models fluid flow and phase separation in membranes, using mathematical analysis and numerical methods. Researchers proved the global existence and uniqueness of weak solutions for the system on a curved surface and developed a discrete finite element method designed to conserve energy and mass. The method incorporates projections to maintain specific properties of the system, and numerical simulations were used to validate the approach and explore phase separation phenomena in geometries like tori and liposomes. These findings contribute to a better understanding and computational modeling of membrane dynamics.

This paper addresses the problem of finding configurations of points in Euclidean space that minimize a squared-stress objective, a common goal in metric geometry. The authors demonstrate that if the dimensionality of the space is one greater than the number of known pairwise distances, any stationary point of this objective will have zero residual stress, resolving a long-standing conjecture. Their proof utilizes a combination of positivity arguments, normalization techniques, and rank-nullity analysis, and the entire theorem has been formally verified using the Lean 4 theorem prover.

This paper addresses the challenge of maintaining accuracy when using irregular, cut-cell grids in finite volume simulations. The authors propose Delta Redistribution, a modification of the State Redistribution technique designed to precisely preserve the steady-state solution while mitigating the issues arising from small cell volumes. The method was tested in two-dimensional simulations and demonstrates the ability to maintain solution accuracy in complex geometries.

This paper addresses the performance bottleneck in matrix-splitting iterative methods, which are limited by memory access rather than computational speed. The authors introduce a mixed-precision technique combining half and double-precision arithmetic to reduce data movement, theoretically demonstrating comparable convergence rates to exact-precision methods. Experiments on various iterative methods and a NASA fluid dynamics simulation (OVERFLOW) showed average speedups of 1.60x and 1.25x for Jacobi and Gauss-Seidel methods, respectively, and a 1.14x speedup for OVERFLOW while maintaining solution accuracy through iterative refinement.

This work addresses the challenge of improving the accuracy of isogeometric analysis (IGA) for solving partial differential equations while retaining its geometric precision. The authors introduce IGA-KAN, a novel method that integrates local, closed-form Kolmogorov-Arnold networks into the IGA framework to refine the solution, rather than replacing the IGA entirely. Through a batched linear least-squares fitting process and an a posteriori error safeguard, IGA-KAN achieved significant reductions in L^2 and H^1 error compared to standard IGA, and substantially outperformed standalone neural network approaches, demonstrating improved performance in both forward and inverse problem scenarios.

This paper investigates the efficiency of midpoint methods for Langevin sampling, a technique used to approximate probability distributions. The authors analyze both deterministic and randomized midpoint discretizations, employing techniques from Malliavin calculus to derive upper bounds on the number of gradient queries needed to achieve a desired accuracy level. Their analysis reveals that deterministic methods, particularly Heun, can outperform randomized methods in high dimensions, while also establishing lower bounds that confirm the efficiency of the deterministic approaches.

This study investigates the challenges encountered when using neural networks for physics-informed machine learning, which aims to solve partial differential equations. Researchers compared neural network representations with B-splines within a physics-informed learning framework, using four problems with known solutions to evaluate their performance. The analysis revealed that B-splines generally exhibited faster convergence rates, lower sampling requirements, and greater robustness compared to neural networks, suggesting potential advantages for certain applications.

This paper addresses the challenge of solving elliptic partial differential equations on complex three-dimensional meshes composed of irregularly shaped cells, a common issue in computational modeling. The authors develop a nonparametric, face-based finite element method that avoids performance degradation often seen with distorted meshes by constructing local approximation spaces independent of mesh geometry. Through theoretical analysis and numerical experiments, they demonstrate the stability and optimal convergence rate of their method, even on severely distorted meshes, by incorporating techniques inspired by discontinuous Galerkin methods to correct for consistency errors. The resulting method provides a robust framework for finite element simulations on highly complex geometries.

This paper introduces a new iterative method, Relaxed Maximum-Based Normal $S$-Iteration (RMNSI), to solve generalized absolute value equations, a class of problems arising in various applications. The approach combines a fixed-point formulation with a relaxation parameter and simplifies computations by reusing a single factorization of a coefficient matrix. Numerical experiments demonstrate that RMNSI achieves competitive efficiency and accuracy compared to existing methods, with the optimal relaxation parameter primarily influenced by the matrix structure rather than problem size.

Alternating projections can exhibit slow convergence when applied near intersections of smooth manifolds with small angles. This paper introduces a framework called Fixed-Point Manifold Acceleration (FPMA) to achieve local convergence and polynomial acceleration of smooth maps that fix a manifold. The authors demonstrate that FPMA yields R-linear convergence and preserves first-order responses to perturbations, with a polynomial acceleration rate of $p(1)=1$, and establish a curvature criterion for second-order retractions. Results show that acceleration improves convergence rates, predicting a reduction in evaluations proportional to $O(θ_F^{-1})$ as the angle approaches zero, a significant improvement over standard alternating projections.

Calculating probabilities in poker tournaments using the Independent Chip Model (ICM) is computationally challenging due to the vast number of possible finishing orders. This paper introduces DE-ICM, a new deterministic algorithm that efficiently computes these placement probabilities by approximating a complex integral representation with a double-exponential quadrature scheme. The algorithm achieves near-exact results, with observed errors as low as $10^{-14}$, and can compute placement matrices for up to 4,000 players in a matter of seconds.

This paper addresses the challenge of efficiently approximating solutions to first-order time-harmonic Maxwell's equations using high-order polynomial spaces. The authors develop a novel approach using quasi-Trefftz spaces, which are designed to maintain high-order accuracy while minimizing the number of basis functions by focusing on smooth solutions. They identify optimal quasi-Trefftz spaces and propose construction methods, demonstrating their effectiveness through theoretical analysis and numerical validation. The resulting spaces offer a more efficient alternative to traditional polynomial spaces for solving Maxwell's equations.

This paper addresses the challenge of developing a robust and efficient numerical method for solving scalar conservation laws. The authors adapt the Total Variation Diminishing (TVD) theory to the Active Flux method, a single-stage approach, to ensure solution stability and accuracy. By deriving a modified version of Harten's lemma and incorporating easily computed parameters, they create a third-order accurate method. The resulting method maintains conservation properties while achieving improved performance compared to lower-order alternatives.

This paper addresses the problem of characterizing the shape of simplices in higher dimensions, extending previous results known for two and three dimensions. The authors demonstrate that the minimum solid angle of a simplex is a shape measure in any dimension and establish inequalities relating this angle to the simplex's fullness. Their findings reveal that the fullness is bounded by the minimum solid angle, with exponents proven to be optimal for dimensions three and above, thereby generalizing the minimum angle condition. The study also provides a comprehensive review of various simplex shape measures and their interconnections.

The paper investigates kernel functions derived from linear stochastic differential equations (SDEs) to incorporate prior knowledge into estimation processes like Gaussian process regression and system identification. The authors leverage a sequentially semiseparable (SSS) representation of the covariance matrix to develop linear-complexity recursive algorithms for key computations, such as factorization and posterior sampling, which are typically computationally expensive. This approach enables efficient matrix operations and provides analytic marginal-likelihood gradients for specific SDE-induced kernels, demonstrating improved performance compared to existing Kalman filtering-based methods. Numerical results validate the accuracy of the proposed algorithms and showcase their utility in posterior inference and sampling.

This paper addresses the challenge of accurately simulating compressible Euler equations, particularly for atmospheric flows, by developing a novel numerical method that preserves key physical properties. The authors construct an entropy-stable and well-balanced discontinuous Galerkin spectral element method, discretizing the equations in a vector-invariant form and utilizing symmetric/antisymmetric products for nonconservative terms. The resulting scheme conserves thermodynamic entropy and total energy while maintaining balance with both isothermal and isentropic background states, demonstrated through several numerical examples showcasing robustness and accuracy.

This paper addresses the challenge of accurately estimating errors in solutions to parametric partial differential equations with nonlinearities, particularly when using neural networks for approximation. The authors develop computable error estimators, designed to function as loss functions for neural networks, by splitting the nonlinear operator and measuring the linear residual in a discrete dual norm, employing a computable surrogate for the dual norm when necessary. They demonstrate that these estimators provide globally reliable and efficient error bounds across the entire trial space, and importantly, they can be used to train neural networks to approximate solutions to these equations.

This paper addresses the challenge of creating neural networks that maintain specific functional properties, such as positivity, during operation. The authors develop a new class of neural network operators that are explicitly designed to preserve a given strictly positive function, analyzing their approximation behavior and providing quantitative error estimates for continuous functions. Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of these operators in preserving exponential and logarithmic functions, and a denoising application highlights their practical utility for modulated signals.

This research addresses the challenge of reconstructing complete physical field data and identifying unknown system parameters when only sparse measurements of a single field are available in a coupled system. The authors developed a machine learning framework utilizing a cross-attention encoder and Fourier neural operator decoder, incorporating physics-based constraints to guide the reconstruction and parameter optimization. Results on several fluid dynamics and magnetohydrodynamics problems demonstrate the framework’s ability to accurately recover unobserved fields and system parameters from limited input data.

This paper addresses the Guided Local Hamiltonian Problem, a computationally challenging task of estimating and preparing a ground state given a guiding state. The authors investigate the Truncated Power Method (TPM), a classical algorithm, and demonstrate its efficiency under the condition that the ground state's $\ell_1$-norm is polynomially bounded. Their analysis reveals that, in this specific regime, TPM's runtime scales similarly to quantum algorithms designed for the same problem, effectively dequantizing those quantum approaches.

This paper addresses the challenge of accurately simulating ultrashort pulse propagation in nonlinear optical media, which requires handling complex interactions between electromagnetic fields and material properties. Researchers developed a family of high-order finite-difference time domain (FDTD) methods that combine advanced spatial and temporal discretizations with a modified exponential integrator to maintain stability and accuracy even with rapidly changing nonlinear effects. The resulting schemes demonstrate theoretical convergence rates and successfully captured nonlinear wave phenomena like soliton propagation in numerical simulations, extending previous approaches to a more computationally efficient FDTD framework.

previous.text: Recent work highlights the potential of revisiting quasi-Newton methods for training deep learning models, including physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), traditionally hampered by computational complexity. A key innovation lies in developing scalable approaches that estimate curvature without expensive matrix operations, enabling improved performance across diverse architectures like recurrent networks and diffusion models. These methods frequently outperform established optimizers like Adam and SOAP, suggesting a path towards more efficient and potentially more accurate PINN training. While the focus is on scalability, the variational objectives used to estimate curvature introduce a new layer of complexity that warrants further investigation. Ultimately, this research signals a promising shift in optimization strategies for PINNs, moving beyond standard approaches to leverage the benefits of quasi-Newton techniques.

summaries: This paper explores using physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) to solve Einstein's equations describing the evolution of black holes, specifically focusing on the moving-puncture method. The researchers developed a neural network architecture that minimizes a loss function incorporating data, the Ricci tensor, and gauge conditions to predict the lapse, shift, and conformal variables of the spacetime. The resulting PINN model successfully interpolated existing numerical relativity data, predicted future evolution, and even reconstructed the interior of a Schwarzschild black hole from exterior data alone, demonstrating a novel approach to solving complex astrophysical problems.

This paper addresses the challenge of accurately estimating errors in numerical solutions to the Uncertain Volatility Model, which is used to price European options. The authors construct a posteriori primal-dual error bounds by combining a feedback control based on the value function's Hessian with a matrix-valued Gamma field to create upper and lower bounds, and then analyze discrete-time approximations of these bounds. Numerical experiments using stochastic policy-gradient and neural network methods demonstrate that accurate second-order derivative information is crucial for generating tight error estimates, particularly when compared to martingale dual approaches.

This paper addresses the challenge of accurately estimating parameters in machining dynamics models that include regenerative delay and nonsmooth friction, both of which complicate traditional modeling approaches. Researchers developed a novel extended physics-informed neural network (XPINN) framework that divides the time domain into segments to improve training and parameter learning. The resulting XPINN method outperformed a standard PINN formulation, demonstrating improved solution reconstruction and parameter estimation, particularly when dealing with extended time periods and variable historical influences, while remaining robust to measurement noise.

This study investigates the effectiveness of adaptive weighting strategies in physics-informed neural network (PINN) training for crystal growth simulations, a process complicated by the need to balance PDE satisfaction with accurate boundary conditions. Researchers compared fixed-weight PINNs, gradient-normalized PINNs, and an adaptive controller (AgenticPINN) on benchmark problems and a simplified crystal growth model. The AgenticPINN reduced PDE residuals significantly but at the cost of increased boundary-condition loss, highlighting the trade-offs inherent in adaptive training and suggesting that overall performance should be assessed using individual error metrics rather than a combined loss function.

Existing wireless digital twins often use ray tracing for scalability, but this method struggles with accuracy when electromagnetic waves diffract or refract, common at sub-6 GHz frequencies. This paper introduces a hybrid approach combining ray tracing with a physics-informed neural network (PE-PINN) to improve accuracy by modeling wave interactions with objects and materials. The framework selectively uses the PE-PINN in areas where ray tracing is inaccurate, achieving results closely matching full-wave simulations while maintaining efficiency and demonstrating practical integration into a wireless digital twin.

The study addresses the challenge of assessing the reliability of slopes with spatially variable soil properties using a novel label-free approach. Researchers developed a physics-informed neural network (PINN) to perform incremental strength reduction and generate numerous random soil profiles, subsequently training a neural operator on the PINN’s output to rapidly predict slope behavior. The PINN accurately reproduced finite element solutions and the neural operator enabled the efficient evaluation of a million slope configurations, demonstrating consistent failure probabilities down to $10^{-3}$. The results highlight the potential of this method to accelerate reliability assessments while underscoring the impact of small factor of safety variations on failure probability.

Physics-informed neural networks struggle with accurate long-time simulations of partial differential equations due to a lack of temporal causality. This paper introduces CEENs, a new method that addresses this by dividing the time domain into subintervals and training separate neural networks sequentially within each interval, enforcing causality through a novel loss function. The resulting method demonstrates improved accuracy and computational efficiency compared to standard PINNs for long-time PDE simulations, and includes a parallelization algorithm for further speedup.

This paper addresses the challenge of ensuring the stability and convergence of physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) by examining the neural tangent kernel (NTK) and gradient descent behavior. The authors develop a method to verify the positive definiteness of the NTK and provide guarantees for finite-width networks, applicable to various linear constraints including differential equations, weak-form residuals, and nonlocal observations. Their approach involves checking a rank condition on a matrix derived from the problem's design, which serves as a certificate for NTK positivity, and allows for explicit determination of network width and step size to ensure geometric loss decrease during training. Experimental validation confirms the effectiveness of the proposed certificates and finite-width mechanism.

Additive friction stir deposition (AFSD) presents a modeling challenge due to the complex interplay of thermal and material flow fields, compounded by the temperature dependence of material properties. Researchers developed a multi-task physics-informed neural network (MCoPINN) to predict velocity and temperature fields in AFSD while simultaneously reconstructing temperature-dependent thermophysical properties from limited data. The resulting model accurately reproduced benchmark finite-volume method simulations and experimental measurements, demonstrating a significant reduction in computational time compared to traditional methods. This approach offers a pathway to efficiently explore a wider range of AFSD process conditions by accounting for variable material behavior.

This paper addresses the challenge of analyzing the accuracy of physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) when applied to complex systems involving both fluid and structural dynamics. The authors develop error estimates for a PINN approximating a coupled heat-wave model, which serves as a simplified representation of fluid-structure interaction problems, by bounding the error using PINN residuals and network parameters. Their analysis demonstrates that the generalization error is directly linked to the training error, the number of quadrature points used, and the network size. The study provides the first error estimates for PINN approximations of this type of coupled PDE system.

Fourier Feature Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) often struggle with uneven convergence rates across different frequencies due to spectral bias. This paper analyzes the training dynamics of these networks to identify that the differential operator influences the convergence of specific frequencies. The authors then propose an initialization strategy that adjusts the initial weight distribution based on the PDE being solved, effectively mitigating this operator-induced spectral bias. Experiments on linear and nonlinear PDEs demonstrate that this operator-informed initialization improves learning dynamics and prediction accuracy without increasing computational cost.

Uncertainty quantification for random partial differential equations is computationally challenging due to the curse of dimensionality. This paper introduces S$^{2}$-PINN, a novel physics-informed neural network that leverages a learnable Gaussian spatial dictionary, Fourier temporal features, and generalized polynomial chaos to represent solutions of random PDEs with a low-rank tensor decomposition. Experiments on manufactured and non-manufactured problems demonstrate that S$^{2}$-PINN achieves superior accuracy in mean and variance estimation, calibration, and parameter efficiency compared to nine baseline methods, suggesting stochastic separability as a promising design principle for neural UQ.

Equation learning using biologically-informed neural networks (BINNs) is hindered by the need for careful hyperparameter selection, which often lacks systematic guidance and limits reproducibility. This study introduces a diagnostic workflow to optimize hyperparameters when ground-truth equations are unavailable, focusing on network capacity, training epochs, and term stability. Through experiments on synthetic systems with known equations, the researchers demonstrate a correlation between validation loss and the error in learned terms, ultimately providing practical rules of thumb for BINN hyperparameter selection. The resulting workflow aims to simplify the application of BINNs for equation learning by offering structured guidance and suggested starting values.

summaries: This paper investigates the use of Kolmogorov-Arnold networks (KANs) to solve free-boundary partial differential equations, which describe problems with interfaces that change during the simulation. The researchers developed a KAN-based solver that incorporates constraints and boundary conditions through residual-based loss functions, testing it on linear and nonlinear elliptic obstacle problems and a Stefan problem. Results demonstrate that KANs achieve high accuracy and effectively resolve contact regions compared to standard physics-informed neural networks, suggesting they offer a promising alternative for these types of simulations.

This paper addresses the challenge of accurately simulating the flow of two immiscible fluids in a thin film using a hyperbolic system of conservation laws. Researchers developed high-order numerical schemes incorporating entropy dissipation, comparing an exact formulation with a simplified approximation for flux evaluation. The study found that while the simplified approach is easier to implement, it results in higher computational costs compared to the more complex exact formulation. Numerical experiments using both finite-difference and spectral element methods revealed that the choice of flux formulation significantly impacts solver efficiency.

This paper addresses the challenge of approximating and computing the geodesic Sinkhorn distance, a Riemannian metric defined on the space of probability distributions. The authors establish convergence results for both spatial discretization using Eulerian methods and temporal discretization of the Sinkhorn divergence, demonstrating how these discretizations approach the underlying energy functional. Based on these theoretical findings, they develop and implement numerical schemes to generate approximations of the geodesic Sinkhorn distance.

Liverani, Saussol, and Vaienti maps present a challenge for numerical analysis due to their slow mixing and lack of spectral gap. To address this, the authors developed a novel numerical method based on Abel functions and asymptotic expansions to accurately estimate properties of the invariant measure, covering both finite and sigma-finite cases. This approach yielded the first practical estimates for parameters far from zero, enabling a deeper exploration of intermittent dynamics. The results are anticipated to facilitate the proof of optimal memory loss rates, a previously unexplored area for systems with infinite invariant measure.

This paper introduces a novel variational framework for diffusion processes within adaptive multiresolution spaces, addressing limitations of traditional methods that rely on fixed approximation spaces. The authors formulate a time-discrete variational principle that simultaneously adjusts the representation, interaction graph, and diffusion operator based on the evolving state of the multiresolution analysis. Numerical experiments, including applications to denoising and imaging, demonstrate the method's ability to localize resolution, achieve high reconstruction quality, and maintain stability with a significantly reduced active representation.

This paper addresses the challenge of efficiently solving numerous parameterized linear systems that arise in many scientific applications. The authors introduce a novel Toeplitz infinite GMRES method that leverages a block upper triangular structure within the Krylov subspace to reduce computational cost and memory requirements, employing incremental recurrences and a generator-refreshing strategy to mitigate numerical instability. Numerical experiments and theoretical analysis demonstrate the efficiency of the proposed methods, with the rebased variant requiring exact matrix-function actions and exhibiting a scaling limitation related to Taylor coefficients.

This paper introduces two particle-based methods for aligning point sets within defined boundaries, leveraging the Fokker-Planck equation. One method uses moving least squares to track particle movement based on a dynamically adjusting particle cloud, while the other employs a Monte Carlo simulation of a related stochastic differential equation to derive registration paths. Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and scalability of both approaches, particularly the latter's suitability for high-dimensional registration tasks. The research offers a novel ghost point method for handling obstacles during the registration process.

This paper addresses the challenge of establishing theoretical guarantees for the convergence of stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics (SGLD), a method used to find solutions to optimization problems. The authors derive asymptotic bias bounds in Wasserstein distance, contingent on assumptions about the problem's convexity, gradient Lipschitz continuity, and the stochastic gradient estimator's error. Their results demonstrate that bias scales with the stepsize, $h$, either as $h$ or $h^{1/2}$, depending on the moment assumptions placed on the gradient error, with a counterexample illustrating the limitations of weaker assumptions.

The study addresses the challenge of accurately simulating wave propagation in complex, two-phase systems with varying material properties. Researchers developed a finite-volume method using a cell-centered approach and perfectly matched layers to handle boundaries, incorporating a volume-fraction representation for material properties. Numerical experiments, including layered gas-liquid transmission and rigid-sphere radiation, demonstrated second-order accuracy for pressure and velocity on orthogonal meshes, with slightly reduced accuracy on non-orthogonal meshes, and validated the method's ability to accurately predict radiation forces. The results provide a quantitative assessment of the method's performance and highlight areas for future refinement.

This paper addresses the simulation of elastic wave propagation across imperfect interfaces between two materials, where the interface introduces a discontinuous displacement field. The authors develop a novel unfitted hybrid high-order method that avoids mesh alignment with the interface by incorporating interface conditions through a regularized stiffness matrix and employing a symmetric strain reconstruction technique. Numerical results in two dimensions demonstrate the method’s ability to achieve convergence rates of order $h^{k+1}$ and $h^{k+2}$ for various high-order approximations, while remaining robust to significant variations in interface compliance.

Dynamo action in fluid mechanics presents significant computational challenges that have motivated a re-evaluation of numerical methods. This paper introduces a finite element exterior calculus (FEEC) approach to compute the spectra and pseudospectra of advection-diffusion operators acting on differential forms, leveraging finite element de Rham complexes. The research develops and analyzes structure-preserving finite element schemes to address these computations, aiming to improve the accuracy and efficiency of dynamo simulations. Results provide a framework for analyzing the spectral properties of these operators within a dynamo context.

This paper addresses the challenge of efficiently solving coupled heat equations arising in conjugate heat transfer, where heat flows between different materials. The researchers employed Dirichlet-Neumann waveform relaxation, a partitioned approach allowing independent subproblem solutions, and developed a fully discrete $l^2$ error analysis using an exponentially weighted Fourier technique. The analysis revealed that convergence behavior is largely independent of spatial grid resolution when using a large CFL number, but depends on the grid ratio when the CFL number is small, and numerical experiments validated the accuracy of the derived error estimates.

This paper addresses the challenge of accurately pricing American options within complex financial models that account for both fluctuating volatility and correlation between assets. The authors extend existing stochastic local volatility models by incorporating a stochastic correlation structure and utilize a reflected forward-backward stochastic differential equation (RBSDE) framework to derive pricing and hedging solutions. Numerical methods were developed and analyzed to solve these RBSDEs, demonstrating the framework's ability to model option price evolution and providing a means to evaluate the performance of the extended models. The results highlight the RBSDE approach's accuracy and efficiency in handling these complex financial scenarios.

Gradient random-walk methods estimate solutions to convection-diffusion equations using signed particles, but suffer from sampling error. This paper introduces sign-switched antithetic coupling, a new pairing strategy where particles of equal sign receive opposite displacements, aiming to reduce variance in the simulation. Numerical experiments on the heat and Burgers equations demonstrate that sign-switched pairing significantly reduces variance compared to independent sampling and reflected pairing, achieving a target mean-squared error with fewer simulations and faster computation times. The results suggest this technique offers a practical improvement for repeated field estimates in particle-based simulations.

This paper introduces a new numerical integration method tailored for high-dimensional spaces, addressing the challenge of accurately computing integrals of non-periodic functions. The approach utilizes a quadrature rule based on transformed lattice points, incorporating periodization and kernel interpolation to approximate the integrand and density functions, with optional subsampling to reduce computational cost. The method achieves a convergence rate of approximately $|J|^{-(α-1/2)}$ and $|J|^{-α}(1.110721)^s$, demonstrating a balance between convergence speed and dimensionality dependence through numerical experiments.

The scalar auxiliary variable (SAV) method, used to approximate gradient flows, can suffer from a loss of positivity in the auxiliary variable, potentially compromising long-term stability. This paper addresses this issue by reformulating the discrete evolution of the auxiliary variable as a convex quadratic equation, ensuring a unique positive root at each time step. The authors demonstrate that this quadratic reformulation, combined with a product-form discretization, preserves positivity while maintaining the original computational cost and energy stability of the SAV method, as validated through numerical experiments on the Cahn–Hilliard equation.

This paper introduces a new numerical method for simulating hydrodynamic flows using a continuous Galerkin, Deferred Correction (cG-DeC) approach on curvilinear staggered grids. The method combines high-order finite element discretization with an explicit time integrator to avoid computationally expensive global matrix inversions, and incorporates a modified hyperviscosity model for shock stabilization. Numerical experiments demonstrate the accuracy and robustness of the cG-DeC scheme, showing improved performance compared to a standard continuous Galerkin Runge-Kutta method.

Landweber iteration is a common method for solving ill-posed inverse problems, but quantifying the uncertainty in reconstructions due to noisy data remains a challenge. This paper develops a statistical interpretation of the Landweber iteration for the Radon transform, linking it to generalized fiducial inference and incorporating a theoretical bias bound to estimate reconstruction uncertainty. To reduce computational cost, the authors use randomized singular value decomposition to approximate the normal operator, carefully accounting for the introduced approximation error in the uncertainty quantification. Numerical results demonstrate the method's ability to provide accurate reconstructions and reliable uncertainty estimates with reduced computational expense.

The paper addresses the challenge of creating simplified, reduced-order models for complex systems described by quadratic-bilinear descriptor equations and multiple inputs. Researchers developed a matrix-free moment-matching method that constructs separate projection spaces for each input channel to capture their individual and combined effects. This approach avoids the need to store large system matrices, making it applicable to computationally intensive problems like fluid dynamics. Results from simulations of two-dimensional flow demonstrate the accuracy of the reduced-order models in replicating the full-order system’s transient behavior under varying inputs.

This paper addresses the challenge of efficiently simulating kinetic equations at low Mach numbers, where computational costs become prohibitive. The authors develop a new hyperbolic relaxation system by decomposing the kinetic equation into macroscopic equilibrium and microscopic non-equilibrium components, deriving a closed system based on orthogonal polynomials. The resulting model, a modified Grad 13-moment system, is shown to be structurally stable and is implemented with a high-order numerical scheme that preserves asymptotic behavior as the Mach number approaches zero. Numerical results demonstrate the scheme’s accuracy, stability, and computational efficiency across a range of physical parameters.

This paper addresses the challenge of learning transport maps between probability distributions when high-quality data are limited. The authors propose multifidelity methods that combine readily available, lower-quality data with scarce high-quality data to construct a bijective map between a reference distribution and a target distribution. They evaluate two strategies for incorporating low-fidelity data—hierarchical and non-hierarchical—and demonstrate that these approaches improve map estimation compared to using only high-fidelity data, ultimately enhancing conditional sampling and uncertainty quantification in a downstream inference task.

The authors developed a family of scalable quasi-Newton methods that estimate positive-definite curvature using variational objectives and leverage stable coupled Newton-Schulz iterations to avoid costly matrix decompositions. Experiments on recurrent networks, autoencoders, physics-informed neural networks, and a large diffusion model demonstrated that SoftServe frequently achieved lower losses compared to popular optimizers like Adam, Muon, and SOAP.

The researchers developed a KAN-based solver that incorporates constraints and boundary conditions through residual-based loss functions, testing it on linear and nonlinear elliptic obstacle problems and a Stefan problem. Results demonstrate that KANs achieve high accuracy and effectively resolve contact regions compared to standard physics-informed neural networks, suggesting they offer a promising alternative for these types of simulations.

The study investigates how symmetry impacts the expressivity and design of geometric quantum machine learning models, specifically quantum Fourier models (QFMs). Researchers utilized the Fourier representation of QFMs to analyze how symmetry organizes the frequency spectrum and developed a symmetrization technique that groups Fourier coefficients based on symmetry orbits. The analysis revealed a relationship between coefficient variances and orbit structure, leading to tighter bounds on Fourier coefficients and demonstrating how orbit growth can prevent expressivity loss, with experimental validation showing improved performance in quantum physics-informed neural networks solving partial differential equations. The work also introduces a randomized encoding method for implementing invariant models efficiently.
